props.text: Last Thursday I read Alice's Adventures in Wonderland on the train. Alice had been swimming in her own tears, and she kept upsetting the Mouse by talking about her cat and then a dog. In Chapter 3, “A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale,” the Dodo announces, “_Everybody_ has won, and all must have prizes.” Asked who gives them, it points to Alice: “Why, _she_, of course,” ([Chapter 3](#)).

Later in Chapter 3, Alice sadly offers her thimble, and the Dodo formally presents it as an elegant prize; Alice thinks the ceremony absurd but accepts it solemnly ([Chapter 3](#)). The awkwardness may lie in the mismatch: she is declared a winner, yet the prize is something she already owned. That seems to echo what you describe about being thanked, as though your own effort is being handed back to you. Since you organise the lunches and usually pay the deposit yourself, perhaps the thanks can feel like a token standing in for recognition of that effort—but that’s only one possibility. Does that fit, or is something else about the moment what feels awkward?

“But she must have a prize herself, you know,” said the Mouse.

“Of course,” the Dodo replied very gravely. “What else have you got in

cheered.

to say, she simply bowed, and took the thimble, looking as solemn as

turns.userMessage: I organise our team's thank-you lunches and usually pay the deposit myself. Everyone says how appreciated I am, but lately the thanks feel oddly like being handed my own effort back. Can you help me separate wanting recognition from wanting somebody else to carry a bit of the work?
turns.reply:
It may help to separate two questions: “Do they see and value what I do?” and “Is this effort still mine to carry alone?” Thanks can answer the first while leaving the second untouched. And when you’ve paid the deposit yourself, appreciation may feel like your effort being reflected back to you rather than anyone taking a piece of it on.

You don’t have to choose between wanting recognition and wanting help; both can be true. To tell which need feels sharper, imagine the next lunch: would it feel more relieving if someone else handled the deposit or another task, even if the thanks stayed the same? Or would being specifically acknowledged make the difference, even if you still organized it?

turns.userMessage: I organise our team's thank-you lunches and usually pay the deposit myself. Everyone says how appreciated I am, but lately the thanks feel oddly like being handed my own effort back. Can you help me separate wanting recognition from wanting somebody else to carry a bit of the work?
turns.reply:
That distinction makes sense: appreciation is about whether people notice and value what you’ve done; shared effort is about whether you’re left carrying the practical load alone. Their thanks may be sincere and still not change who organizes the lunches or pays the deposit.

One way to untangle it is to imagine each need being met separately. If someone thanked you warmly but you still handled the planning and deposit, would something feel missing? And if someone took a concrete piece off your plate without much praise, would that feel relieving—or would recognition still matter too? You may want both, in different ways. Which imagined change feels like it would address the sharper part of this lately?
